verification.title: Scholia to Homer's Odyssey, Book 10 (Σχόλια εἰς Ὀδυσσείας κ' / Схолии к «Одиссее», песнь X): Aeolus, the Laestrygonians, Circe and Elpenor
verification.ru_found: I could not refute the claim that there is no Russian translation of the book-10 scholia. Method: 2 WebSearch queries ("схолии к Одиссее перевод Цирцея моли"; "\"схолии к Одиссее\" перевод с древнегреческого"). Both returned nothing relevant. The session's WebSearch budget (200/200) then ran out, so I did about 16 targeted queries in the CyberLeninka catalog API instead: схолии к Одиссее, схолии Одиссея перевод, лестригоны схолии, Кирка Одиссей схолии, Кратет Малльский, Порфирий Гомеровские вопросы, Эльпенор, Эол мех ветров, мифограф Гомера, схолии перевод Гомер, Гераклит Аллегории Гомера, Аристарх Одиссея, Евстафий Одиссея, and others. None of them turned up a translation of any Odyssey scholia, let alone book 10. I also checked the raw HTML of the ancientrome.ru Homer page (ancientrome.ru/antlitr/homer/index.htm). It lists only the Greek texts, the Gnedich/Veresaev translations, the Homeric Hymns and Felenkovskaya's dictionary, with no scholia. One warning: the WebFetch summarizer wrongly reported "Схолии к Одиссее … Жуковским" on that page, and the raw HTML shows this is false. Two related Russian translations exist, but they translate other texts, not the scholia: (1) А. В. Гараджа, «Аллегории Михаила Пселла I (перевод и комментарии)», Scholae 2025 (cyberleninka.ru/article/n/allegorii-mihaila-psella-i-perevod-i-kommentarii). It includes Psellos' allegory on Odysseus and Circe (Od. 10), made from the Duffy 1992 and Littlewood 1985 editions. (2) А. В. Гараджа, «"О Стиксе" Порфирия Тирского (перевод и комментарии)», Scholae 2025 (cyberleninka.ru/article/n/o-stikse-porfiriya-tirskogo-perevod-i-kommentarii). It translates the Stobaeus fragments, which include the metempsychosis reading of Circe's transformations (Stob. 1.49.60 = Plu. fr. 200 Sandbach) and cite Od. 10.212–13, 10.277 and 10.509–15. Both are useful for cross-reference in a commentary. I did not verify whether «Античные теории языка и стиля» or Losev's anthologies contain any Odyssey-10 scholia; I believe they do not, but that is from memory.
verification.en_found: Of the whole book-10 corpus, only one scholion is available in English. Camden Roy and R. Scott Smith, "Mythographical Narratives (historiai) in the D scholia to the Odyssey" (Canopos/Manto-Myth 2026, CC BY 4.0, from Ernst's Greek text), is also on ToposText as work 921 (topostext.org/work/921). Its book-10 content is a single entry, § 10.494 (Teiresias' change of sex and his prophetic gift after death). The section list jumps from 3.91 to 10.494 to 11.266, so there is nothing on Aeolus, the Laestrygonians, Circe, moly or Elpenor. I confirmed this on both the ToposText page and the Canopos catalog page. I found no English translation of the scholia corpus for book 10 (Aristonicus/Didymus/Herodian/Nicanor material, V/D glosses, the Crates–Aristarchus note on 10.86, Porphyrian zetemata). Two English WebSearch queries returned nothing relevant before the budget ran out. Isolated scholia may be quoted in English in secondary works (e.g. Nünlist 2009, Dickey 2007), but I could not check this. On the label: the colleague's "partial" and my "excerpts_only" rest on the same evidence; one D-scholion out of about 1,374 lemma entries is an excerpt, not a partial translation.
verification.other_found: Catalan: Sergi García Prat, "Edició crítica dels escolis al cant X de l'Odissea" (UAB doctoral thesis, Sept. 2022; supervisors J. Cors i Meya and J. Pàmias). I downloaded and read the PDF. Contents: introduction, state of the question, witnesses, codices, edition method, stemma, critical edition (pp. 48–259), index, bibliography. It gives the Greek text with a negative apparatus and testimonia (Eustathius, Etymologicum Magnum, Porphyry) and no translation. The companion thesis on book 9 by E. Ramírez Sevilla (2016, ddd.uab.cat/record/176016) is also Greek only, per the SERMN description. J. Cors i Meya, "Les aventures d'Ulisses i els escolis a l'Odissea", Faventia 30 (2008) 97–103, is a programmatic article with no translation. Italian: F. Pontani, Scholia Graeca in Odysseam vol. V (July 2022, books 9–10, per García Prat p. 11) is a critical edition, not a translation. I found no Italian, French, German, Spanish or Modern Greek translation of the book-10 scholia. Further searches were not possible because the WebSearch budget was used up, so isolated quotations in, for example, Broggiato's Italian edition of Crates (2001) remain unchecked.
verification.source_text: Primary base: S. García Prat, Edició crítica dels escolis al cant X de l'Odissea (UAB 2022), CC BY-SA 4.0. Record: https://ddd.uab.cat/record/273918; PDF (7.4 MB, 305 pp.): https://ddd.uab.cat/pub/tesis/2023/hdl_10803_688122/sgp1de1.pdf. It collates 45 manuscripts. The Greek is real Unicode (EB Garamond) and extracts cleanly with PyMuPDF, although some spaces are dropped after accented words. I counted about 1,374 lemma entries on 529 verses, about 23,000 Greek words, with 19 Porphyry and 191 Eustathius parallels flagged. Public-domain cross-check: W. Dindorf, Scholia Graeca in Homeri Odysseam, Oxford 1855, vol. 2, which contains book K (archive.org/details/scholiagraeodyss02homeuoft, "NOT_IN_COPYRIGHT"; the Greek OCR is noisy). For the D/V layer: N. Ernst, Die D-Scholien zur Odyssee (Köln 2004), KUPS urn:nbn:de:hbz:38-18313, kups.ub.uni-koeln.de/1831/. It is free to access, but the page says only "Rights: user, author, copyright", not CC. For Porphyry: H. Schrader, Porphyrii Quaestionum Homericarum ad Odysseam pertinentium reliquiae (1890, public domain). Pontani vol. V (2022) is in copyright and should be used only for consultation and comparison of readings; García Prat notes gaps in its manuscript coverage, at κ 121 and κ 483.
verification.recommendation: This is a strong candidate. Nothing in Russian or any other language translates the book-10 scholia corpus, English has only the single D-scholion on 10.494, and an openly licensed, machine-readable critical text exists (García Prat 2022, CC BY-SA). A good pilot is Od. 10.80–132, the Laestrygonians, including the 10.86 'short nights' debate between Crates and Aristarchus; a second unit could be Circe and moly, 10.210–347, with Porphyry and Eustathius parallels and Garadzha's 2025 Russian Psellos and Porphyry 'On the Styx' translations as cross-references.

verification.title: Scholia to Odyssey 23.296–24.548: the 'end' (τέλος/πέρας) of the Odyssey and the Second Nekyia (reports of Aristophanes of Byzantium and Aristarchus via Aristonicus/Didymus; MSS H M Q V, Vind. 133)
verification.ru_found: No Russian translation of these scholia turned up, either in full or as excerpts. Seven Russian-language searches were run: "схолии к Одиссее перевод"; "гомеровские схолии перевод на русский Аристоник Дидим"; "вторая Некийя Аристарх атетеза схолии"; "конец Одиссеи Аристарх 23, 296"; "Аристарх ... Аристофан Византийский XXIV песнь подлинность"; a cyberleninka-targeted query on book 24 as a late addition; and a combined query on "схолии к Одиссее" plus "конец поэмы". All of them returned either English scholarship (CHS, GRBS, sententiaeantiquae, Cambridge) or general Odyssey pages (livelib, bigenc.ru). The only Russian academic hit was an MSU Lomonosov-2015 conference abstract on Homeric quotations in Plutarch's De audiendis poetis (aspirant.msu.ru). It mentions Dindorf's Odyssey scholia but translates nothing from books 23–24. One lead is still open: the new Russian Odyssey translated by Grigory Starikov (Nosorog / Jaromír Hladík press, 2026; reported by Meduza, 14 July 2026, https://meduza.io/feature/2026/07/14/...) comes with a large commentary on mythology, etymology and translation choices. It is not known whether that commentary quotes the 23.296 scholion, so it should be checked physically. Not checked at all: Hyperboreus, Philologia Classica, ΣΧΟΛΗ, Аристей, ВДИ, Лосев's «Гомер» and Н. П. Гринцер's work on Alexandrian exegesis. These are the most likely places for a passing quotation of the telos scholion. Nothing indicates a continuous translation.
verification.en_found:
No continuous English translation of the scholia on 23.296–24.548 was found. The colleague's label "partial" is better described as "excerpts only". What exists:
(1) Joel Christensen's blog Sententiae Antiquae (29 Jan 2016, https://sententiaeantiquae.com/2016/01/29/where-does-the-odyssey-end-and-why-aristarchus-aristotle-and-eustathius/; reused 9 Dec 2020, https://sententiaeantiquae.com/2020/12/09/are-peace-and-wealth-enough-ending-the-odyssey-odysseyrtw/). It gives Greek and English, translator uncredited (presumably the blogger), for only the short scholia on 23.296 (ἀσπάσιοι λέκτροιο; Ἀριστοφάνης δὲ καὶ Ἀρίσταρχος πέρας τῆς Ὀδυσσείας τοῦτο ποιοῦνται; τοῦτο τέλος τῆς Ὀδυσσείας φησὶν Ἀρίσταρχος καὶ Ἀριστοφάνης), together with Aristotle, Poetics 1455b and Eustathius on the Odyssey (Stallbaum II.308).
(2) Gregory Nagy, 'Odyssey 24' (Harvard continuum.fas.harvard.edu/?p=19445) only paraphrases the 23.296 report and translates no scholia. The CHS page 'The End of the Odyssey' (classics-at.chs.harvard.edu) refused connection and could not be checked.
(3) Stephen Bertman, 'Structural Symmetry at the End of the Odyssey', GRBS (text extracted from the PDF) cites the scholia M V Vind. 133 and H M Q on πέρας/τέλος in a footnote, without translating them.
(4) Stephanie West, 'Laertes Revisited', PCPhS 35 (1989) 113–143, discusses the 23.296 scholion and the objections to book 24. Whether it translates them could not be confirmed.
Not verified from this session but very likely: the standard commentaries paraphrase or partly translate Aristarchus' arguments against the Second Nekyia (scholion on 24.1). These are Heubeck's commentary on book 24 in the Oxford Commentary vol. III (1992; Italian original in the Fondazione Valla Odissea vol. VI) and Stanford, Hermathena 100 (1965). Neither is a translation of the scholia. One caveat on the search count: the session's WebSearch budget ran out after about 8 calls, so only 2 explicitly English searches ran instead of the required 4. The English picture is backed up by the direct page fetches listed here.
verification.other_found: No French, German, Italian or Spanish translation of this block of scholia was found, and the search budget ran out before targeted searches in those languages could be run. Pontani's critical edition, Scholia Graeca in Odysseam (Edizioni di Storia e Letteratura, 2007–), gives Greek text with a Latin apparatus and no translation. On present knowledge it has not reached books 23–24, though its 2026 status could not be re-checked. Likely partial treatments to check, all unverified here: G. Petzl, Antike Diskussionen über die beiden Nekyiai (Meisenheim 1969), a German study of the ancient debate on the Second Nekyia that probably quotes the scholia on 24.1 at length; Heubeck's Italian commentary on book 24 in the Fondazione Valla Odissea vol. VI (1986); and H. Erbse, Beiträge zum Verständnis der Odyssee (1972). These are commentaries or studies, not translations of the scholia.
verification.source_text:
Primary source: W. Dindorf, Scholia Graeca in Homeri Odysseam, vol. II (Oxford 1855). It is on archive.org as https://archive.org/details/scholiagraeodyss02homeuoft, marked NOT_IN_COPYRIGHT; the volume runs to p. 844 and includes the scholia on books ψ–ω. This is currently the only complete edition of the old (H M Q V and other) scholia for books 23–24.
Cross-checks, all public domain:
- A. Carnuth, Aristonici περὶ σημείων Ὀδυσσείας reliquiae emendatiores (Leipzig 1869), for the Aristarchean signs and atheteses at 23.310–343 and in book 24.
- A. Ludwich, Aristarchs homerische Textkritik (Leipzig 1884–85), vol. I, Odyssey section, for Didymus and the Aristarchean readings.
For the D-glosses on 23–24: N. Ernst, Die D-Scholien zur Odyssee. Kritische Ausgabe (Köln, KUPS), open access at http://kups.ub.uni-koeln.de/1831/1/D-Scholien.pdf. The repository gives the year as 2004, while the brief cited 2006; the edition is open access either way. Ernst covers only the D-scholia, not the Aristarchean/Didymean notes.
Pontani's edition is in copyright and is not yet available for these books.
verification.recommendation: Strong Neoscholia candidate: no Russian translation was found, and English has only a few one-line excerpts of the 23.296 scholion. The block is a compact, well-known crux, and the public-domain Dindorf 1855 text can be checked against Carnuth and Ludwich. Start with a dossier on the "end of the Odyssey": the two versions of the 23.296 τέλος/πέρας scholion, the athetesis notes on 23.310–343, and the long scholion on 24.1 with Aristarchus' arguments against the Second Nekyia (a few Dindorf pages). Optionally add Eustathius on 23.296 alongside. Then extend to the rest of book 24 (Laertes, the ending).

verification.title: Aristonicus, Περὶ σημείων Ὀδυσσείας (On the Critical Signs of the Odyssey), fragments ed. Carnuth 1869
verification.ru_found: I found no Russian translation, either full or partial. Two Russian searches ran: "Аристоник «О знаках» Одиссеи перевод" and "Аристарх атетезы Одиссеи схолии Аристоник". Neither turned up a Russian translation, an anthology excerpt or an article giving Aristonicus' Odyssey notes in Russian; the results were only general Odyssey pages (bigenc.ru, livelib, a Meduza piece on a new Odyssey translation) and Western scholarship. Caveat: the session's web-search budget (200 calls) ran out after these two Russian queries. My planned searches on ancientrome.ru, ΣΧΟΛΗ, Hyperboreus and Philologia Classica ("Аристарх Самофракийский Одиссея схолии перевод", "александрийская филология критические знаки Аристоник") could not be run. The "none" verdict is likely correct but rests on thinner Russian coverage than the task required.
verification.en_found: There is no full or systematic English translation. The Perseus Catalog (urn:cts:greekLit:tlg1194.tlg001) lists only Carnuth's 1869 Greek edition, with no translation: https://catalog.perseus.org/catalog/urn:cts:greekLit:tlg1194.tlg001 . The main modern English work on Aristarchus' signs covers only the Iliad: Schironi's Classical Quarterly article "Aristarchus' work in progress: what did Aristonicus and Didymus read of Aristarchus?" explicitly limits itself to Iliad scholia and calls the Odyssey scholia "much more heterogeneous" (https://www.cambridge.org/core/journals/classical-quarterly/article/aristarchus-work-in-progress-what-did-aristonicus-and-didymus-read-of-aristarchus/BB820B34D79D5C97A32C0CCEBEC0A651). This refutes "none" only in a narrow sense: individual Aristarchean Odyssey notes do circulate in English. Verified example: the Sententiae Antiquae blog post "Where Does the Odyssey End (and Why?) Aristarchus, Aristotle and Eustathius" gives Greek with English renderings of the scholia on Od. 23.296, for example "Aristarchus and Aristophanes claim this as the end (telos) of the Odyssey". The translator is not named on the page (https://sententiaeantiquae.com/tag/emendation/). Scattered translated or paraphrased notes probably also appear in Odyssey commentaries and in Nagy's CHS essays on Aristarchus, but I did not verify these individually. The Canopos/ToposText D-scholia translation (Roy & Smith) covers mythological narratives, not Aristonicus' material on the signs.
verification.other_found: I found no French, German, Italian or Spanish translation of the Aristonicus Odyssey collection. The 19th-century German work (Carnuth 1869; Ludwich, Aristarchs homerische Textkritik 1884–85) is Greek text with Latin or German discussion, not a translation. Pontani's Scholia Graeca in Odysseam (2007–, in copyright) re-edits the Aristonicus-derived scholia in Greek only. Because the search budget ran out, I could not run dedicated Italian or Spanish searches, so smaller translated excerpts in Italian scholarship such as Pontani's studies on the Odyssey scholia cannot be ruled out. Status for those: unknown.
verification.source_text: The base text is Otto Carnuth, ed., Aristonici Περὶ σημείων Ὀδυσσείας reliquiae emendatiores (De signis Odysseae), Leipzig: S. Hirzel, 1869, about 172 pp. It is marked "Not in copyright" on archive.org: https://archive.org/details/perisemeionodyss00arisuoft (PDF, page images, full text). The fragments run by Odyssey book and line, with a Latin preface and Latin notes and no translation. The archive.org Greek OCR is poor (broken accents and breathings, Latin letters substituted for Greek), so the Greek needs fresh OCR or manual checking from the page images. For context, two public-domain companions help: Dindorf, Scholia Graeca in Homeri Odysseam (1855), and Ludwich, Aristarchs homerische Textkritik (1884–85; archive.org aristarchshomer00gramgoog). Carnuth's text is outdated, so for books 1 onward that Pontani's edition covers, it should be checked against Pontani (in copyright, for checking only, not reproduction).
verification.recommendation: Strong candidate. No Russian translation was found, and English has only scattered single-note renderings (e.g. Od. 23.296), so the "untranslated" claim mostly holds; English should be marked "excerpts_only", not "none". Start with Carnuth's entries for Books 23–24 (Aristarchus' "end of the Odyssey" at 23.296), which is short and of high interest. Then do Book 11, the Nekyia atheteses, and print each Odyssey line with its note so the terse, technical entries make sense.

verification.ru_found: I found no Russian translation, either full or partial. Searches run: WebSearch for «схолии к Одиссее перевод песнь IX Циклоп» and «схолиаст Одиссея Полифем "Никто" схолии перевод»; Brave for «схолии к Одиссее перевод Циклоп», «"схолии к Одиссее" перевод» and «схолии Гомер Полифем Марон вино схолиаст»; the CyberLeninka API for 7 queries («схолии Одиссея» 130 hits, «схолии к Одиссее» 109, «схолиаст Одиссея» 62, «Полифем схолии» 6, «Киклоп Одиссея» 37, «схолии Гомер перевод» 218, «Евстафий Одиссея» 87); and the ancientrome.ru Homer index, which lists only Zhukovsky's Odyssey and editions, with no scholia. None of these turned up a translation of the Od. 9 scholia. Closest item: B. A. Kayachev, «Odyssea 9, 31: damnavit Propertius», Индоевропейское языкознание и классическая филология, 2009 (cyberleninka.ru/article/n/odyssea-9-31-damnavit-propertius-propertsiy-3-12-23-38). It quotes and discusses single scholia (on Od. 9.32 and 9.403) in Greek as part of an argument; that is scholarly citation, not a translation. Yandex and DuckDuckGo returned CAPTCHAs, which were not bypassed. I could not check printed anthologies (e.g. «Античные теории языка и стиля», Losev) against their full text, but nothing indicates they contain Od. 9 scholia.
verification.en_found: The colleague's claim that there is no English translation at all is refuted at the excerpt level. There is no complete or systematic English translation. Found: the blog Sententiae Antiquae (sententiaeantiquae.com) has published English translations, with the Greek, of individual Book 9 scholia. (1) Schol. ad Od. 9.106, the long scholion on how many eyes the Cyclops had and Polyphemus' parentage, which includes Aristotle's discussion (roughly 450–800 words). Posted 2017-04-04, reposted 2018-07-19 (https://sententiaeantiquae.com/2018/07/19/how-many-eyes-did-the-cyclops-have-the-answer-might-surprise-you/), 2020-12-08 and 2021-07-14. (2) Schol. ad Od. 9.195, on Odysseus taking twelve men so as not to look like pirates (about 200 words). Posted 2017-04-09 (https://sententiaeantiquae.com/2017/04/09/odysseus-doesnt-want-to-be-mistaken-for-a-pirate/). (3) Lotus-Eater scholia: Schol. T 9.89, Q 9.92 and HQ 9.97. Posted 2019-04-20 and reposted (https://sententiaeantiquae.com/2019/04/20/drugs-the-homeric-scholia-and-the-lotus-eaters/); related posts 2017-04-08 and 2019-01-05 / 2020-09-02. Confirmed absent: ToposText work 921, the D-scholia Odyssey mythographic narratives translated by Roy & Smith (2026, CC-BY, from Ernst's text). Its full list of sections jumps from 3.91 to 10.494, so there are no Book 9 entries. Possibly also exists, not verified here because the search budget ran out: short translated quotations in secondary works, e.g. the Aristotle Homeric Problems fragment preserved in schol. Od. 9.106 in studies of Aristotle's Homeric Problems, or scholia-criticism handbooks such as Nünlist's. Related, but not the scholia themselves: the online Cullhed & Olson translation of Eustathius on the Odyssey adds about two books a year (books 1–4 reported online) and has not reached Book 9. The Cambridge 'Ancient Scholia to Homer's Iliad' translation covers the Iliad only.
verification.other_found: No French, German, Italian, Spanish or Catalan translation found. Ramírez Sevilla, «Edició crítica dels escolis al cant IX de l'Odissea» (UAB doctoral thesis, 2016, 237 pp., 37 manuscripts, major and minor scholia), is an edition only. Its introduction (§1.1) explicitly excludes translation and commentary as outside the thesis's scope and leaves them for future work. Checked in the PDF: https://ddd.uab.cat/pub/tesis/2016/hdl_10803_400698/ers1de1.pdf. The companion thesis for Book 10, García Prat 2022 (ddd.uab.cat/record/273918, CC BY-SA 4.0), is likewise an edition. Pontani, Scholia Graeca in Odysseam V: Scholia ad libros ι–κ (Rome, Edizioni di Storia e Letteratura, «Pleiadi» 6.5, 2022; confirmed in Pontani's Lincei bibliography) is a Greek critical edition, in copyright. The BMCR review of vol. I mentions no translation, and nothing indicates that any volume includes one. (One search-engine summary said the volumes have Italian translations; I could not confirm this and believe it is wrong.) Cors i Meya, Faventia 30 (2008), is a programmatic article on editing the scholia to Books 9–12, with no translation.
verification.source_text: Primary, public domain: W. Dindorf, Scholia Graeca in Homeri Odysseam, Oxford 1855, vol. II. Book Ι (9) is in vol. II; the OCR of vol. I shows it ends with Book Θ. Internet Archive scholiagraeodyss02homeuoft (marked NOT_IN_COPYRIGHT): https://archive.org/details/scholiagraeodyss02homeuoft. Other scans: bub_gb_vjRyAAAAIAAJ, scholiagrcainho00homegoog. Minor/D layer, open access: N. Ernst, Die D-Scholien zur Odyssee. Kritische Ausgabe (Köln, thesis 2004, online on KUPS), https://kups.ub.uni-koeln.de/1831/. Collation aid: Ramírez Sevilla 2016 (ddd.uab.cat/record/176016). The DDD record says CC BY-NC-ND 3.0, but the thesis's TDX notice is more restrictive, and the ND clause makes it unsuitable as a base for a published translation. Use it only to check readings. Pontani vol. V (2022), in copyright, is the authoritative modern text and should be consulted for readings and attributions, not reproduced.
verification.recommendation: This is a strong candidate: no Russian translation exists, and English has only a handful of blog-translated scholia (9.89, 9.92, 9.97, 9.106, 9.195). A full annotated RU/EN translation of the Book 9 scholia would be new. Start with the Cyclopean-ethnography block (scholia on Od. 9.105–135, including the long zetema at 9.106), then do the Outis/Mētis and blinding block (9.355–414). Base it on Dindorf 1855 plus Ernst's D-scholia, and acknowledge the Sententiae Antiquae translations of 9.106 and 9.195 in the notes.

verification.title: Κράτητος Μαλλώτου λείψανα: Crates of Mallos, Homeric fragments on the Odyssey (Кратет Малльский, фрагменты об «Одиссее»)
verification.ru_found: There is no Russian translation of the fragments as a collection. Searches for "Кратет Малльский фрагменты перевод" and "Кратет из Малла Гомер эфиопы Океан аллегория" found none, and ru.wikipedia "Кратет Малльский" lists no translation, only the Lübker dictionary entry (1885) and Wachsmuth 1860. This still refutes "none": the central Odyssey fragments that come down through Strabo are in Russian inside G. A. Stratanovsky's complete translation of Strabo's Geography. The mybook.ru text of Book I names Stratanovsky and contains Crates passages, for example «Толкование Кратета более правдоподобно» on Homer's Ocean (https://mybook.ru/author/strabon/geografiya/read/). Strabo 1.2.24–31, which covers the debate between Crates and Aristarchus over the twofold Ethiopians (Od. 1.23–24) and the torrid zone filled by Ocean, is therefore available in Russian. The following come from memory and were not confirmed by fetching: the 1964 date of the Stratanovsky edition; Gellius 14.6.3 (inner sea per Aristarchus vs outer Ocean per Crates for Odysseus' wanderings) in the Russian «Аттические ночи», books XI–XX, published by Гуманитарная академия in 2008; Sextus Empiricus, Adv. math. 1.79, in Losev's Russian Sextus; and Suetonius, De grammaticis 2, in Gasparov's translation. A Russian version of Geminus 6 (the Laestrygonians' short nights) is unverified. Fragments preserved only in the scholia on the Odyssey and Iliad have no Russian translation.
verification.en_found: There is no English translation of the collection. Porter's BMCR review (2003.11.33, https://bmcr.brynmawr.edu/2003/2003.11.33/) confirms Broggiato 2001 has 143 numbered fragments "but no translations" and wishes it had full translations. Gregory Nagy's 2025 essay "About Crates of Mallos" (https://continuum.fas.harvard.edu/about-crates-of-mallos/) discusses fragments, mostly on the Iliad, and does not translate a corpus. The key Odyssey fragments still exist in English inside the authors who preserve them. Strabo 1.2.24–40 (Ethiopians, Crates vs Aristarchus, Ocean in the torrid zone) is in the Loeb translation by H. L. Jones (1917, public domain), online at LacusCurtius: https://penelope.uchicago.edu/Thayer/E/Roman/Texts/Strabo/1B2*.html. Duane W. Roller's 2014 Strabo is also available (from memory). Geminus, Introduction to the Phenomena, which includes the Crates passage on the Laestrygonians, has a complete English translation by J. Evans and J. L. Berggren (Princeton 2006/2007; https://press.princeton.edu/books/hardcover/9780691123394/geminoss-introduction-to-the-phenomena). Gellius 14.6.3 is in Rolfe's Loeb (1927), from memory. Scholarly articles probably translate selected fragments, for example Porter's "Hermeneutic Lines and Circles" in Lamberton and Keaney (eds.), Homer's Ancient Readers (1992), and Romm's The Edges of the Earth (1992), but this was not verified. The fragments preserved only in the scholia remain untranslated.
verification.other_found: Italian: Broggiato, Cratete di Mallo: I frammenti (La Spezia: Agorà, 2001) gives Greek text and commentary with no translation (BMCR 2003.11.33). Broggiato, Filologia e interpretazione a Pergamo. La scuola di Cratete (Sapienza, 2014) edits Crates' followers, not Crates himself. Pontani, Sguardi su Ulisse (2005; BMCR 2005.09.40) surveys Odyssey exegesis and may paraphrase Crates; not a translation, unverified. BMCR 2021.03.56 (Perrone, "Cratete") is about the comic poet Crates and is not relevant. Translations of the host authors exist but were not fetched: German Strabo (Radt 2002–11), German Geminus (Manitius, Teubner 1898, Greek with German translation, public domain), French Strabo (Budé, Aujac/Lasserre 1969), Italian Strabo (Biraschi, BUR). Mette's Sphairopoiia (1936) is a study and edition; whether it includes a German translation is unknown. No French, German or Spanish translation of the collected fragments was found.
verification.source_text: Public domain: C. Wachsmuth, De Cratete Mallota (Leipzig: Teubner, 1860), confirmed at https://archive.org/details/decratetemallot00wachgoog (PDF and full text available). Each fragment should be checked against its source: W. Dindorf, Scholia Graeca in Homeri Odysseam (Oxford, 1855); the Kramer or Meineke Strabo (or Jones' Loeb 1917 Greek text); Manitius' Geminus (Teubner, 1898); and Gellius in Hosius (Teubner, 1903). For modern numbering and readings use M. Broggiato, Cratete di Mallo: I frammenti (2001), which is in copyright and should serve only as reference and concordance.
verification.recommendation: This is a good secondary candidate. Nobody has published a collected, annotated Russian or English translation of Crates' Homeric fragments, but the best-known Odyssey items (Strabo 1.2.24–31, Gellius 14.6.3, Geminus on the Laestrygonians) are already readable in Russian and English inside Strabo, Gellius and Geminus, so the label should be "excerpts only", not "none". Start with an "Odyssey dossier" of Crates: the fragments on the Odyssey from Wachsmuth 1860, keyed to Broggiato's numbers and ordered by book (1.23–24 Ethiopians, 10.82–86 Laestrygonians, the wanderings in the outer Ocean, and so on). Lead with the fragments preserved only in the scholia, which are truly untranslated, and cross-reference the existing Strabo, Gellius and Geminus translations.

verification.title: Scholia to Odyssey 1.1–309, auctiora (major, minor/V, D and Byzantine scholia; proem, divine council, Athena-Mentes, Phemius) — Схолии к «Одиссее» I
verification.ru_found: I found no Russian translation of the Odyssey 1 scholia, either as a corpus or for single scholia. Searches covered: 6 WebSearch queries in Russian (схолии к Одиссее перевод; πολύτροπος/Антисфен/Порфирий; "схолиях к Одиссее"; Нахов «Антология кинизма»; Лосев/Тахо-Годи «гомеровские схолии») plus 12 queries through CyberLeninka's own search API. Those API queries returned only unrelated items: Файер on Zenodotus and Aristarchus (Iliad); Ермолаева on Od. 19.560; Богданова on Homeric quotations in the Hesiod scholia (Шаги 2024); and Гараджа's ΣΧΟΛΗ translations of Proclus' Chrestomathy, Psellus' Allegories and Porphyry's On the Styx. None of these translates schol. Od. 1. One gap is open: the Antisthenes passage in schol. Od. 1.1 (SSR V A 187 = DC 51) might be in Russian in И. М. Нахов, «Антология кинизма» (1984/1996), but I could not get the book's contents online to check. Even if it is there, it would be one excerpt only.
verification.en_found:
The "untranslated" claim is partly wrong for English. There is no full or systematic English translation of the scholia to Od. 1.1–309, but the most important scholion in the unit is translated:
(1) Schol. Od. 1.1, Porphyry reporting Antisthenes on πολύτροπος (SSR V A 187), is translated in full in Susan Prince, Antisthenes of Athens: Texts, Translations, and Commentary (Univ. of Michigan Press 2015), t. 187, pp. 591–3. It is also translated in G. Boys-Stones and C. Rowe, The Circle of Socrates (Hackett 2013), t. 1.21, pp. 12–13. Both are confirmed by the bibliography of Dotto 2025 (see other_found).
(2) The blog Sententiae Antiquae has English translations of schol. Od. 1.1, including the long HM scholion attributed to Porphyry (https://sententiaeantiquae.com/2017/06/11/many-meanings-for-many-wayed/; repost 2020/12/08), and of schol. E Od. 1.2 on πτολίπορθος (https://sententiaeantiquae.com/2018/02/11/achilles-can-sack-cities-or-how-aristarchus-can-be-wrong/).
(3) ToposText 921 (Roy & Smith 2026, D-scholia to the Odyssey from Ernst's text) has no book-1 entries; its first entry is on Od. 3.4. This confirms the sweep.
Short quotations of single scholia in monographs are likely but I did not verify them for specific lines. Nothing covers the Zeus theodicy (1.32ff.), the Ethiopians, Athena-Mentes or Phemius in any systematic way.
verification.other_found:
Portuguese: Pedro Mauricio Garcia Dotto, «Odisseu πολύτροπος: tradução e comentário de um fragmento de Antístenes de Atenas», Classica (Brazil) 38 (2025). It gives the Greek with a full Portuguese translation of the Antisthenes part of schol. Od. 1.1, on Prince's text. URL: https://classica.emnuvens.com.br/classica/article/download/1124/1309/5026
Spanish: a translation of SSR V A 187 is likely in M. Mársico, Filósofos socráticos II (2014), which Dotto cites, but I did not check that it is there. No Spanish translation of the scholia corpus found. The Spanish CSIC Odyssey (Valverde and García López 2022) uses the scholia only in its critical apparatus. The UAB theses are critical editions of the scholia to books 9 (Ramírez Sevilla) and 10 (García Prat 2022), with no translation and not book 1.
Italian: Pontani's Scholia Graeca in Odysseam I (α–β, 2007) is a Greek critical edition with no translation (BMCR 2008.07.39). No Italian translation found. I could not check whether Pontani's Sguardi su Ulisse (2005) translates any scholia.
German: none found.
French: none found, but my French search did not run because the session's web-search limit was reached, so this is unknown rather than verified.
verification.source_text:
Public domain:
- W. Dindorf, Scholia Graeca in Homeri Odysseam, vol. 1 (Oxford 1855), marked NOT_IN_COPYRIGHT on archive.org: https://archive.org/details/scholiagraeodyss01homeuoft (another copy: scholiagraecain06dindgoog). It covers all of book α but is thin and unreliable for 1–309 (Pontani has about 86% material not in Dindorf).
- A. Ludwich, Scholia in Homeri Odysseae α 1–309 auctiora et emendatiora (Königsberg program fascicles, 1888–90). This is the best public-domain text for the unit. Correction to the sweep: archive.org item scholiainhomerio00ludw has only 20 pages and contains just the fascicle for α 44–63 (1888), even though its catalogue title reads "A 1-43, A 64-309". The other fascicles were not found on archive.org. They may be on HathiTrust or Google Books (both blocked my checks), or in the Olms reprint (1966).
- Openly licensed: N. Ernst, Die D-Scholien zur Odyssee. Kritische Ausgabe (Köln 2004/2006), open access: https://kups.ub.uni-koeln.de/1831/
Reference only (in copyright): F. Pontani, Scholia Graeca in Odysseam I (Rome 2007), the scholarly standard, with about 26% more notes than Ludwich on 1–309. Italian law gives critical editions 20 years of protection (L. 633/1941 art. 85-quater), which may matter for 2027 or later. Check this with a lawyer.
verification.recommendation: This is a strong candidate. There is no Russian translation and no translation in any language of the unit as a whole. English (Prince 2015; Boys-Stones & Rowe 2013) and Portuguese (Dotto 2025) cover only the Porphyry/Antisthenes scholion on πολύτροπος, so the English status should be "excerpts_only", not "none". Start with the proem block, schol. Od. 1.1–21, adding the already-translated Antisthenes scholion as a cross-referenced first Russian version. Then do 1.22–95 (Ethiopians, Zeus' theodicy, Aegisthus). Base the text on Dindorf 1855 plus whatever Ludwich fascicles can be found, with Pontani 2007 as a control text.

verification.ru_found: I found no Russian translation, full or partial. Searches run: WebSearch "Евстафий Солунский комментарий к Одиссее перевод" and "Евстафий Фессалоникийский «Одиссее» пещера нимф комментарий Порфирий". Ten Russian queries through the CyberLeninka search API, including "Евстафий Фессалоникийский Одиссея комментарий", "Евстафий Солунский Гомер перевод", "схолии к Одиссее перевод", "Евстафий Порфирий пещера нимф", "феакийский корабль окаменение" and "византийские комментарии к Гомеру перевод". I also checked the ancientrome.ru library index (no Eustathius entry), simposium.ru and the Russian Wikipedia article, which lists no Russian translations. Closest hits, none of them a translation: (1) Р. С. Соловьев, «Гомер как первый богослов: аллегория и символ в трактате Порфирия „О пещере нимф“», Вестник ПСТГУ III: Филология 64 (2020) 47–66 (https://cyberleninka.ru/article/n/gomer-kak-pervyy-bogoslov-allegoriya-i-simvol-v-traktate-porfiriya-o-peschere-nimf). Note 31 paraphrases in one sentence Eustathius' verdict that Porphyry said much nonsense about the cave in elegant words (cited as Eust. Comm. ad Od. 2.41.35–36 Stallbaum). That is a passing paraphrase, not a translated excerpt. (2) А. В. Гараджа, «О Стиксе» Порфирия (ΣΧΟΛΗ 19.1, 2025) only cites Eust. In Od. 1658 (book 10). Side finding for the project: Garadja also published «Аллегории Михаила Пселла I» (ΣΧΟΛΗ 19.2, 2025), a Russian translation of Byzantine Homeric allegory that is relevant elsewhere. Caveat: my WebSearch budget ran out after 2 of 4 planned Russian WebSearch queries. The Russian check therefore leans on CyberLeninka; elibrary.ru and print anthologies were not checked directly.
verification.en_found: There is no modern English translation of the Book 13 commentary. Cullhed and Olson (Brill) cover only the following: vol. I (preface and books 1–4, 2022), vol. II (5–8, 2023) and vol. III (9–12, 2026, ISBN 9789004727946, 655 pp.; https://andromedabooks.gr/?p=308096). The Brill Scholarly Editions online version (DOI 10.1163/2772-3216, subscription only) has the same coverage. Library descriptions (TAU database 3451) say "books 1-12 now available, work ongoing". BMCR 2023.11.38 (Mastronarde) names no translation earlier than Cullhed's 2016 edition of books 1–2. I found no listing anywhere for vol. IV (books 13–16). REFUTATION OF "EN none": the notes to Pope's Odyssey (vol. III, London 1725, mostly by Broome) contain English paraphrases of Eustathius' Book 13 comments, which I confirmed in the archive.org OCR (https://archive.org/details/homerpopeodyssey03). They are: (a) the note on the cave ("Porphyry (observes Eustathius) is of opinion, that the cave means the world..."), a long paraphrase of Eustathius' summary of Porphyry's allegory; (b) the note on the Phaeacian city and mountain ("as Eustathius observes it was artful in the Poet to leave this point doubtful..."). The van Goens 1765 'Collectanea ad Porphyrium De antro nympharum' reprints Eustathius alongside the Pope and Dacier observations. These are free 18th-century paraphrases of a few passages and do not cover the commentary.
verification.other_found: I found no French, German, Italian, Spanish or Modern Greek translation of the Book 13 commentary, and no Latin translation of the Odyssey Parekbolai. Possible but UNVERIFIED: Mme Dacier's 'L'Odyssée d'Homère' (Paris 1716), whose remarks are known to draw heavily on Eustathius and are cited together with Pope in van Goens 1765, probably has French paraphrases of a few Book 13 comments; my archive.org search for it returned no results. Italian studies of Byzantine Homeric allegory may quote single passages, but I could not check them because the WebSearch budget ran out. verification.source_text:
**Main public-domain text:** W. Dindorf, Scholia Graeca in Homeri Odysseam, 2 vols, Oxford 1855.
- archive.org: https://archive.org/details/scholiagraeodyss01homeuoft and .../scholiagraeodyss02homeuoft, with OCR djvu text available.
- It prints a ὑπόθεσις at the head of each book, often two. Dindorf's notes ("Utramque ὑπόθεσιν habet O") show the hypotheseis come from codex O, which is Ernst's Z (Bodl. Auct. V.1.51), the main D-manuscript.
- The D-material sits inside Dindorf's mixed V/vulgate scholia and has to be separated out using Ernst's edition.

**Best modern text:** N. Ernst, Die D-Scholien zur Odyssee, KUPS Köln 2004/2006, https://kups.ub.uni-koeln.de/1831/ (PDF: https://kups.ub.uni-koeln.de/1831/1/D-Scholien.pdf).
- The abstract confirms the D-scholia include glosses, "book summaries" and myth summaries.
- It is open access, but the record states no CC licence. As a scholarly edition it may still be protected in Germany (§70 UrhG, roughly to 2029–31). Use it for collation, not for wholesale republication.
- Its PDF text layer uses a non-Unicode Greek font: extraction gives gibberish, so it needs OCR.

**Additional checking:** Pontani's in-copyright edition can be used for checking the books it covers.
verification.recommendation: The claim survives an adversarial check. There is no Russian translation, and the only English one (Roy & Smith 2026) covers just the 44 mythographic historiai. The glosses and the 24 book hypotheseis are untranslated in any modern language I could reach. Start with all 24 Odyssey hypotheseis as one short, complete unit (Dindorf 1855, checked against Ernst's Z). Then do the Book 1 D-glosses as a bilingual Greek–RU/EN glossary with commentary on school method; glosses mean little without the Greek beside them.

General web search was unavailable: the search budget was used up and Google, Bing, DuckDuckGo and Yandex were captcha-blocked or returned junk.

The sweep is confirmed and made more precise. There is no complete English translation of the Homeric Problems fragments.

(1) J. Barnes and G. Lawrence, 'Fragments', in J. Barnes (ed.), The Complete Works of Aristotle: The Revised Oxford Translation, vol. 2 (Princeton 1984). This is a selection. I checked it with the archive.org full-text search, which shows short snippets. In the Homeric Problems section it includes the Odyssey fragments 170 (Calypso mixing nectar for Hermes, Od. 5.93), 171 (αὐδήεσσα: Calypso, Circe, Ino), 172 (how Polyphemus can be a Cyclops) and 175 (the Cattle of Helios, Eustathius' 'allegorical' version). There are no hits for 169 (Pharos/Naucratis), 173 (the Phaeacians), 174 (Poseidon), 176 (Telemachus and Penelope), 177 (Argos the dog) or 178 (refusing Calypso's immortality). Ross's Select Fragments (1952) leaves the Homeric Problems out entirely.
(2) R. Mayhew, Aristotle's Lost Homeric Problems: Textual Studies (OUP 2019), DOI 10.1093/oso/9780198834564.001.0001. Chapter 10 discusses Odyssey 12 (Sirens, Wandering Rocks, Cattle of Helios), with the author's own translations of the texts discussed (his stated practice in his related articles). The reviews are BMCR 2020.05.43 (Novokhatko), CR 2019 (Rinon) and Ancient Philosophy 2020 (Janko). In Hyperboreus 2019 (https://bop.unibe.ch/Hyperboreus/article/view/12122) Mayhew writes 'If I were preparing an edition of the fragments…'. That suggests no new edition or translation had appeared as of 2019. I did not check later years.
(3) For the Phaeacian sleep, the English translation is under Heraclides: Schütrumpf et al., Heraclides of Pontus: Texts and Translation (2008). It is not an Aristotle fragment.
(4) MacPhail 2011 covers Porphyry on the Iliad only.
(5) ToposText/Canopos D-scholia to the Odyssey (Roy and Smith 2026) cites Aristotle only on the Ancaeus proverb at Od. 22.9, which belongs to the Samian Constitution, not the Homeric Problems.

verification.recommendation: This is a valid but very small Russian-first candidate: about 10 Rose fragments (169–178), roughly 3 pages of Greek. English is only partial (Barnes and Lawrence give 4 of the 10, and Mayhew covers Book 12), while German is complete (Breitenberger 2006). The best unit is a single dossier of all Odyssey-related Aristotle fragments from Rose 1886, cross-checked against the original scholia (Dindorf, Schrader). Ideally it would serve as the opening part of a larger translation of Porphyry's Odyssey questions (Schrader 1890), rather than stand alone.

verification.recommendation: This is a valid but niche candidate: I could not find any translation into Russian, English or another modern language, and the source text is public domain. It is very technical, though: notes on punctuation and syntax that only make sense alongside the Greek verse. Start with the Carnuth fragments on Odyssey book 1 (or one speech-heavy book, such as Book 11). Precede them with a translated introduction on Nicanor's 8-mark system based on schol. Dion. Thr. Keep the Greek lemmata and Nicanor's technical terms in both translations.

name: Philosophical, allegorical, ethical and rhetorical reflections on the Odyssey in Greek and Latin antiquity
overview:
Russian coverage of this strand is better than expected. The main allegorical treatises are already in Russian: Heraclitus' Homeric Problems (Marantidi 2018, apparently complete), Porphyry's Cave of the Nymphs (Taho-Godi 1988; Chernigovsky 1996) and On the Styx (Garadja 2025), and Numenius (Afonasins 2009). Plutarch's De audiendis poetis and Gryllus, Dio Chrysostom Or. 53/55, Macrobius' Saturnalia and the opening of Proclus' In Remp. essay 6 (Kroll I.72–86) are also translated. Garadja's RSF-funded project (23-18-00971) on Porphyry's Homeric writings is active, so check it before starting any Porphyry work.

Real Russian gaps:
- Ps.-Plutarch, De Homero (no translation)
- Porphyry's Homeric Questions (no translation)
- Philostratus, Heroicus (no translation)
- Maximus of Tyre Or. 4/17/26 (only Or. 2, 5 and 36 exist)
- most of Proclus' essay 6
- the fragments of Crates of Mallos
- Aristotle's Homeric Problems (status unknown)
- the Latin school scholia on Horace Ep. 1.2

English covers almost all the Greek treatises: Keaney–Lamberton 1996; Maclean–Aitken 2001; Rusten–König 2014; Trapp 1997; Lamberton 2012; Baltzly et al. 2018; Prince 2015 for Antisthenes. Three items have no English translation either: Porphyry's Odyssey questions (MacPhail covers the Iliad only and Schlunk only Vatican Book I), Crates (Italian only, Broggiato 2001), and Porphyrio/Ps.-Acro.

Suggested flagship pair:
- Porphyry's Odyssey Questions: no translation in any language; public-domain text in Schrader 1890.
- Ps.-Plutarch, De Homero: no Russian translation; public-domain text in Bernardakis 1896.

Antisthenes' 'polytropos' fragment is best done inside the Porphyry pilot, since it survives in Porphyry's question on Od. 1.1.

verification.ru_found:
The claim that no Russian translation exists is wrong. There is no full or systematic Russian translation, but some Porphyrian Odyssey zetemata have been published in Russian.
(1) CONFIRMED (I read the PDF): Е. В. Афонасин, «Гераклид Понтийский о поэтах и музыкантах», ΣΧΟΛΗ 14.2 (2020) 742–755, DOI 10.25205/1995-4328-2020-14-2-742-755, https://classics.nsu.ru/schole/14/14-2-heraclid-2.pdf. It translates Heraclides frs. 101–104 Schütrumpf, which are full Porphyrian zetemata on the Odyssey. Each is headed «Порфирий, Гомеровские вопросы к «Одиссее»», and they cover Od. 2.51, 2.63, 11.309 (Otus and Ephialtes vs Tityus) and 13.119 (the sleeping Odysseus and the Phaeacians), all by Schrader's pages. It also translates two Iliad zetemata (2.649, 3.236). Od. 11.309 falls inside the proposed unit.
(2) CONFIRMED, adjacent but not the Homeric Questions (HQ): А. В. Гараджа, «О Стиксе» Порфирия Тирского, ΣΧΟΛΗ 19.1 (2025) 468–488, RSF grant 23-18-00971. It also translates the dubious frs. 381–383 F Smith, including the Stobaeus Circe allegory (Stob. 1.49.60). It cites HQ only from Sodano and Schrader and names no Russian HQ translation. His later ΣΧΟΛΗ translations (Psellus, Allegories I–II, 2025–26) are not HQ. The project is translating Porphyry's Homerica, so an HQ translation from it is possible later.
(3) Russian study, not a translation: Л. И. Щеголева, «Из истории античной филологии: «Гомеровские вопросы» Порфирия Тирского», in «История литературы»: ненаучные истоки научного жанра (ИМЛИ РАН 2022) 161–179, DOI 10.22455/978-5-9208-0684-0-161-179. It covers Vatican Book I only. The PDF returned 401, so I could not check whether it quotes translated passages.
(4) ru.wikipedia (Порфирий) lists no Russian HQ translation. Сидаш's Порфирий, Сочинения (2011) and Труды I–III (Квадривиум 2017–22): the 2011 contents shown do not include HQ, and I could not check the contents of vols. I–III. Нахов, Антология кинизма (1984), pp. 97–133 on Antisthenes: whether it includes the Od. 1.1 polytropos fragment is UNVERIFIED.
verification.en_found:
No complete English translation of Schrader's Odyssey reliquiae exists. MacPhail 2011 (De Gruyter, TK 36) covers the Iliad only (BMCR 2011.06.02), and Schlunk 1993 (Peter Lang) covers Vatican Book I only (BMCR 1994.09.18, Slater). But several zetemata in the proposed unit have been translated, embedded in fragment collections of the authorities Porphyry cites.
(1) CONFIRMED (full text checked): Susan Prince, Antisthenes of Athens: Texts, Translations, and Commentary (Univ. of Michigan Press 2015, ISBN 978-0-472-11934-9). Its t. 187 is a full English translation of the Porphyrian scholium on Od. 1.1 polytropos (also at Il. 9.305). It also translates the Porphyrian scholia on Od. 23.337, 5.211, 7.257 and 9.33 (t. 188); on the Cyclops at Od. 9.106–7, 127, 275 and 411 (t. 189); and on Od. 9.525 (t. 190, Schrader p. 94–95). This is most of the Antisthenean material in the proposed Od. 1.1 + Od. 9 unit.
(2) Prince notes that MacPhail's 2007 Michigan dissertation (Proecdosis of Porphyry's Homeric Questions on the Iliad) includes the Od. 1.1 polytropos passage at pp. 272–77.
(3) E. Schütrumpf (ed.), translated by P. Stork, J. van Ophuijsen and S. Prince, Heraclides of Pontus: Texts and Translation (RUSCH 14, Transaction 2008; Routledge reissue 2018, DOI 10.4324/9780203790151). It contains the same Porphyrian zetemata on Od. 2.51, 2.63, 11.309 and 13.119 in English.
(4) R. Mayhew, Aristotle's Lost Homeric Problems (OUP 2019, DOI 10.1093/oso/9780198834564.001.0001). Its ch. 10, 'Aristotle's Naturalistic Interpretation of Odyssey 12', discusses the Sirens, the ambrosia-bearing doves and the Cattle of the Sun. These are Porphyry-transmitted problems, and the chapter very likely translates them, but I did not see the text.
(5) Probable but not verified (access was restricted): Barnes (ed.), Complete Works of Aristotle, vol. 2 (1984), Fragments section, 'Homeric Problems'; and W. J. Kennedy, Antisthenes' Literary Fragments (PhD thesis, Sydney 2017, open access; title known from the ΣΧΟΛΗ 11.2 review by Protopopova and Garadja).

German, probable but not verified: Flashar, Dubielzig and Breitenberger, Aristoteles: Fragmente zu Philosophie, Rhetorik, Poetik, Dichtung (Akademie 2006, DOI 10.1524/9783050048901). Its 'Literaturwissenschaft… Übersetzungen' section (pp. 289–323) should include the Aporemata Homerica, many of which come from Porphyry's Odyssey zetemata.
Spanish, checked and negative: Vallejo Campos, Aristóteles, Fragmentos (Gredos 2005) follows Ross's selection and does not include the Homeric Problems.
I found no translation of the whole Odyssey reliquiae in any language, and no announced one.
Method note: the WebSearch budget ran out on the first call. Instead I used Crossref bibliographic queries (6 Russian, more than 8 English, plus Italian and German), Internet Archive catalog and full-text checks, ΣΧΟΛΗ tables of contents for 2025–26, BMCR and Wikipedia. Russian web-only resources were therefore under-searched: ancientrome.ru (which has no Porphyry section), simposium.ru, elibrary and the Нахов anthology text.
verification.source_text:
Main text: H. Schrader, Porphyrii Quaestionum Homericarum ad Odysseam pertinentium reliquias (Leipzig: Teubner 1890), public domain. Scans: https://archive.org/details/porphyriiquaest00porpgoog and https://archive.org/details/bub_gb__LwzAQAAMAAJ.
Cross-check the scholia context against W. Dindorf, Scholia Graeca in Homeri Odysseam (Oxford 1855), public domain (https://archive.org/details/scholiagraeodyss01homeuoft, …02homeuoft). For Od. 1.1, use A. Ludwich, Scholia in Homeri Odysseae α 1–309 auctiora et emendatiora (1888–90), public domain.
Schrader is 'antiquated and muddled' and includes non-Porphyrian matter (Slater, BMCR 1994.09.18). Each zetema's attribution and text should therefore be checked against F. Pontani, Scholia Graeca in Odysseam (2007–, in copyright), which supplies the modern text and Porphyrian attributions for the books it covers, and against Prince 2015 and Schütrumpf 2008. Those two give modern texts of the Antisthenes and Heraclides items.
Vatican Book I (Sodano 1970) and MacPhail 2011 are in copyright.
verification.recommendation: This is still a strong Neoscholia candidate: no complete Russian or English translation of Schrader's Odyssey reliquiae exists. But the proposed unit (Od. 1.1 + Od. 9–12) overlaps most with what is already translated: Od. 1.1 and the Od. 9 Cyclops cluster (Prince 2015, Dotto 2026), Od. 11.309 (Afonasin 2020 in Russian; Schütrumpf 2008 in English) and Od. 12 (Mayhew 2019). Start instead with the Porphyrian zetemata on Od. 10–12 (Aeolus, Circe and moly, the Nekyia, the Sirens), cite and footnote the existing partial translations, and keep watching Garadja's RSF 'Homerica' project for overlap.

candidates.author: Pseudo-Plutarch (anonymous)
candidates.genre: Didactic treatise: Homer as source of rhetoric, philosophy and the sciences
candidates.size: 218 chapters; Bernardakis VII pp. 329–462 (c. 130 Teubner pp.)
candidates.edition: Kindstrand, Teubner 1990 (standard). Bernardakis, Moralia VII (1896), PD: https://archive.org/details/in.ernet.dli.2015.103631. Dübner 1855.

candidates.en_evidence: J.J. Keaney & R. Lamberton, [Plutarch] Essay on the Life and Poetry of Homer (Scholars Press 1996, American Classical Studies 40); BMCR 1996.11.14.

candidates.pilot_unit: Philosophical section on the soul and the Odyssey (c. chs. 122–134, incl. Circe ch. 126), c. 10 pp.; then the whole work.

verification.ru_found: I found no full or partial Russian translation of the work. Only isolated passages and paraphrases exist. Under «О жизни и поэзии Гомера (Псевдо-Плутарх)» its only entry is «Демокрит 1970, фр. 170». That is one testimonium in С. Я. Лурье, «Демокрит. Тексты. Перевод. Исследования» (Л., 1970). I could not open the Лурье volume itself to confirm it (https://ru.wikipedia.org/wiki/Моралии_(Плутарх)). (2) Over 12 Russian queries on the CyberLeninka API turned up no translation and no article containing one. Queries included «Псевдо-Плутарх О жизни и поэзии Гомера», «Псевдо-Плутарх Гомер перевод», «жизнеописания Гомера перевод», «"Жизнь Гомера" перевод», «Псевдо-Плутарх аллегория Гомер», «De Homero», «Ps.-Plut. Vit. Hom.» and «Псевдо-Плутарх тропы фигуры Гомер». The journals searched included ΣΧΟΛΗ, Hypothekai, Philologia Classica and ИЯКФ. (6) Russian Wikipedia's «Псевдо-Плутарх» article names the work but gives no translation. Summary for Russian: no translation of the work exists, only at most one doxographic fragment.
verification.en_found: Two complete English translations exist. (1) J. J. Keaney & R. Lamberton, [Plutarch], Essay on the Life and Poetry of Homer (American Classical Studies 40; Atlanta: Scholars Press, 1996). It is a bilingual Greek–English edition of all 218 chapters (BMCR 1996.11.14, J. Holoka: https://bmcr.brynmawr.edu/1996/1996.11.14/; Classical World review DOI 10.2307/4352244). (2) The sweep missed an earlier complete translation that is public domain: 'The Life and Poetry of Homer' in The Complete Works of Plutarch, vol. 6, Essays and Miscellanies (New York: T. Y. Crowell, 1909), translated by Dr W. Lloyd Bevan. BMCR calls it the only earlier English translation. I checked the archive.org text: it runs from ch. 1 to the closing chapter, about 173k characters (https://archive.org/details/completeworks06plut ; also essaysmiscellani0000unse_s6g6). (3) There is also a partial translation: M. L. West, Homeric Hymns, Homeric Apocrypha, Lives of Homer (Loeb 496, 2003). It has '(Pseudo-)Plutarch, On Homer (II)' only on pp. 414–417, which covers the biographical opening alone (DOI 10.4159/dlcl.plutarch-homer_ii.2003). ToposText (checked its works API), Perseus and the OGL First1KGreek repository (checked GitHub, tlg0094 and tlg0007) do not have the work. verification.source_text: The standard critical edition is J. F. Kindstrand, [Plutarchi] De Homero (Leipzig: Teubner, 1990), which is in copyright. The best public-domain Greek text is G. N. Bernardakis, Plutarchi Chaeronensis Moralia vol. VII (Leipzig: Teubner, 1896). 'Περὶ τοῦ βίου καὶ τῆς ποιήσεως Ὁμήρου' begins at p. 329; the OCR is usable but noisy. It is at https://archive.org/details/in.ernet.dli.2015.103631 (archive.org dates it 1888, but the title page reads MDCCCXCVI). A second public-domain option is F. Dübner, Plutarchi fragmenta et spuria (Paris: Didot, 1855), with Latin translation, at https://archive.org/details/ploutarchouapos00dbgoog; I have not opened the scan to confirm the De Homero pages. A public-domain English text for checking is the Bevan 1909 translation (archive.org/details/completeworks06plut). No openly licensed digital TEI edition exists in Perseus or OGL.
verification.recommendation: This is a good candidate for a Russian-only translation: nothing beyond a single Democritus testimonium exists in Russian. It is not a candidate for English (two complete translations, one of them public domain), and there are full Spanish and Italian versions. Start with the Odyssey-heavy soul doctrine, roughly chs. 122–128 (Circe's metamorphoses, the Nekyia, the soul's pneuma), then extend over the philosophical part (chs. 92–160). Translate from Bernardakis 1896, checked against Kindstrand 1990 and the Keaney–Lamberton, Hillgruber and Ramelli apparatus.

candidates.title: Ἡρωικός — Philostratus, Heroicus (On Heroes) — Флавий Филострат, «Героик» («О героях»). Unit: Odysseus/Homer critique sections
candidates.author: Flavius Philostratus
candidates.genre: Sophistic dialogue; revisionist criticism of the Trojan saga and of Homer
candidates.size: c. 58 chapters, c. 60 Teubner pp.; pilot c. 12 pp.
candidates.edition: de Lannoy, Teubner 1977 (standard). Kayser 1870–71, PD: https://archive.org/details/flaviiphilostrat02phil
candidates.ru_evidence: No Russian translation found. A.V. Belousov's 2010 MSU dissertation on the Heroicus cites none, and ru.wikipedia 'Филострат' names the dialogue without a translation.
candidates.en_evidence: Maclean & Aitken, Flavius Philostratus: Heroikos (SBL WGRW 1, 2001); Rusten & König, Loeb 2014 (BMCR 2014.12.33).
candidates.other_translations: Other modern versions were not verified in this sweep.
candidates.odyssey_focus: The hero Protesilaus 'corrects' Homer: Odysseus as Palamedes' murderer and Homer's favourite; Homer's interview with Odysseus' ghost on Ithaca, which buys silence about Palamedes; Odysseus as 'Homer's plaything' in his wanderings. candidates.value: The chief ancient anti-Odysseus revision and meta-critique of Homeric authority. Connects hero cult, the Second Sophistic and Homeric criticism. No Russian translation.
candidates.ai_feasibility: High. Atticist prose of moderate length, with two annotated English versions to check against.
candidates.pilot_unit: Palamedes–Odysseus sections and Homer's encounter with Odysseus' ghost (c. Her. 33–34, 43; numbering to verify), c. 12 pp.

verification.title: Flavius Philostratus, Heroicus (Ἡρωικός, "On Heroes"; Russian «Героик» / «О героях» / «Рассказ о героях»). Unit: the sections where Protesilaus critiques Homer and Odysseus
verification.ru_found:
I partly refuted the sweep's claim that there is no Russian translation. There is no complete Russian translation, but excerpts exist.
(1) V. V. Latyshev's collection «Известия древних писателей греческих и латинских о Скифии и Кавказе» includes Philostratus' «Рассказ о героях», translated by П. И. Прозоров. One online copy prints the initials as Н. И. The excerpts are V,3 (Kayser p. 300: Cyrus and the Massagetae) and XIX,16–20 (Kayser pp. 327–331). Those sections cover Achilles' island Leuke, Achilles' song to Homer, the story of the girl he tore apart, and the Amazons' attack, which is roughly de Lannoy 54–57.
- It was reprinted in ВДИ 1948 № 2. Dissercat cites it as «Филострат. О героях // ВДИ.- 1948. №2. Перевод П. И. Прозорова»: https://www.dissercat.com/content/kulty-drevnegrecheskikh-geroev-akhilla-i-gerakla-v-severnom-prichernomore-vi-i-vv-do-ne
- It was reprinted again in Scythica et Caucasica, т. 1, СПб. 1992.
- An online copy of the text is at https://proza.ru/2009/06/11/201. Studfile and apsnyteka.org quote it as «Филострат Младший. Рассказ о героях XIX 16. Пер. П.И. Прозорова».
- None of these excerpts touches Homer, Odysseus or Palamedes.
(2) A. V. Belousov's studies quote passages in his own translation: «Почему Протесилай? Героика Флавия Филострата и воскресший герой» (ИЯКФ XII, 2008; https://cyberleninka.ru/article/n/pochemu-protesilay-geroika-flaviya-filostrata-i-voskresshiy-geroy) and the monograph «Флавий Филострат в религиозном контексте своего времени: „Жизнь Аполлония“ и „Героика“» (ПСТГУ, 2012). Makhlayuk's review on cyberleninka says the monograph's Appendix 3 gives the text and a translation of Dialexis 2, not the Heroicus. Its chapter III §2 discusses Philostratus' critique of Homer and may quote some of those passages in Russian; I could not check this. Belousov's 2010 dissertation footnote lists only Spanish, Italian, German and English translations.
(3) Russian Wikipedia's «Филострат Старший» lists Russian translations of the Life of Apollonius, Lives of the Sophists, Pictures and Letters, but none of the Heroicus.
(4) A Google AI answer claimed a partial translation by С. П. Кондратьев in ВДИ 1948 № 2. I found no support for that name; the ВДИ 1948 № 2 excerpt is Prozorov's Latyshev material.
Result: there is no Russian translation of the Homer/Odysseus/Palamedes sections or of the whole dialogue that I could find.
verification.en_found:
The English status is confirmed as full, with several versions.
(1) J. K. Berenson Maclean & E. B. Aitken, Flavius Philostratus: Heroikos (SBL Writings from the Greco-Roman World 1, Atlanta 2001), and Flavius Philostratus: On Heroes (WGRW 3, 2002/2003). This translation is free online:
- ToposText: https://topostext.org/work/222, "used by permission of the Society of Biblical Literature". The Odysseus/Homer material is at ToposText §§ 693–695 ("Protesilaos calls Odysseus Homer's plaything"), §§ 708–715 (Palamedes against Odysseus) and §§ 727–729 (Homer sails to Ithaca and summons Odysseus' ghost).
- Harvard Center for Hellenic Studies: chs.harvard.edu, "Flavius Philostratus, On Heroes". The site would not connect when I tried it; ToposText says the full text is there.
(2) J. Rusten & J. König, Philostratus. Heroicus, Gymnasticus, Discourses 1 and 2 (Loeb Classical Library 521, Harvard UP 2014). BMCR 2014.12.33 (https://bmcr.brynmawr.edu/2014/2014.12.33/) says "The first published English translation of Heroicus was that of Maclean and Aitken."
verification.other_found:
- French: Simone Follet, Philostrate, Sur les héros. Collection des Universités de France, série grecque 531, Les Belles Lettres, Paris 2017. This is a new critical text with translation (CCIV + 348 pp.), reviewed in L'Antiquité Classique 88 (2019) and REA.
- German: P. Grossardt, Einführung, Übersetzung und Kommentar zum Heroikos von Flavius Philostrat, 2 vols (Schweizerische Beiträge zur Altertumswissenschaft 33, Basel 2006). Also A. Beschorner, Helden und Heroen, Homer und Caracalla: Übersetzung, Kommentar und Interpretationen zum Heroikos des Flavios Philostratos (Bari: Levante, 1999).
- Italian: Valeria Rossi (ed.), Filostrato, Eroico, with Greek facing text, preface by M. Massenzio (Il Convivio, Venezia: Marsilio, 1997).
- Spanish: Francesca Mestre, Filóstrato, Heroico; Gimnástico; Descripciones de cuadros; Calístrato, Descripciones (Biblioteca Clásica Gredos 217, Madrid 1996).
So the dialogue is fully translated into English, French, German, Italian and Spanish.
verification.source_text:
- Best openly licensed text: C. L. Kayser (ed.), Flavii Philostrati Opera, vol. 2 (Leipzig: Teubner, 1871), which is public domain. The Perseus Digital Library has a TEI/EpiDoc transcription under CC BY-SA 4.0:

  - Scaife viewer: https://scaife.perseus.org/library/urn:cts:greekLit:tlg0638.tlg004/ (cited by Olearius pages)

Only Russian is missing (Latyshev/Prozorov covers just the Leuke and Amazon excerpts); English, French, German, Italian and Spanish all have full translations, and the English one is free on ToposText. Start with a Russian pilot of the Homer–Odysseus–Palamedes cluster (ToposText §§ 693–695, 708–715 and 727–729; roughly de Lannoy ch. 25, 33–34 and 43 — the de Lannoy numbers are approximate) from the CC BY-SA Perseus Kayser text, then consider the first complete Russian Heroicus.

- J. Davis & J. Markland, London 1740
- J. J. Reiske, Leipzig 1774–75 (archive.org bub_gb_k9kVlNtxwGIC)

verification.recommendation: Good Russian-only candidate: it would be the first Russian version of Maximus' three Homer orations, and they are short (about 25 pages in Trapp's translation). Start with Or. 26 (Homer the Philosopher, with Odysseus' wanderings read as the path of virtue), then Or. 17 and Or. 4 as a "Homer trilogy". It fails the "ideally untranslated" test, though: there are three English translations (including the new Loeb) and complete Italian, Spanish, German and French ones. It is also worth checking with Garadja and Belikov, who are translating Maximus into Russian, to avoid overlap.

An older complete translation by F. G. Mishchenko (1879) is public domain.
(3) Athenaeus, translated by N. T. Golinkevich (Nauka 2003 and 2010; books IX–XV in 2010). This includes 11.490e, Crates on the Pleiades doves (Od. 12.62 = F 59).

It contains at least the following, in Rose³ numbering: F 144 (Athenaeus), F 149 (Porph. on Il. 3.277, Helios needing a messenger about his cattle), F 160, F 161, F 166 (Iliad), and four Odyssey fragments. These are F 170 (schol. Od. 5.93, Calypso mixing nectar), F 171 (schol. Od. 5.334), F 172 (schol. Od. 9.106, how Polyphemus can be a Cyclops) and F 175 (Eustathius 1717 on Od. 12.130, the cattle of Helios). Rose³ fr. 173–174 and 176–179 do not appear, so this is a selection. (2) R. Mayhew, Aristotle's Lost Homeric Problems: Textual Studies (OUP 2019; DOI 10.1093/oso/9780198834564.001.0001). It is a set of studies, not a complete translation. name: Byzantine commentaries, allegories, paraphrases and school texts on the Odyssey
overview:
Byzantine work on the Odyssey is the least translated part of this strand. In Russian there is almost nothing beyond Psellos' six Homeric allegories (Garadja, ΣΧΟΛΗ 2025–26) and older chronicle excerpts from Malalas. No Russian version was found for Eustathius' Parekbolai, Tzetzes' Allegories of the Odyssey, Tzetzes on Lycophron, or Gabalas' Odyssey works.

English: Cullhed & Olson (Brill) now cover Eustathius' preface and books 1–12: vol. I 2022, vol. II 2023, vol. III (books 9–12) dated Dec 2025/2026. The online edition also stops at book 12, and completion is projected for 2030 (six volumes). Books 13–24 (Stallbaum 1826, public domain) are therefore the largest block of Byzantine Odyssey commentary still untranslated into any modern language. Tzetzes' Allegories of the Odyssey has a full English translation (DOML 56, 2019). Tzetzes on Lycophron exists only as an English machine translation (ToposText).

Gregoras: no separate text by him was found. The treatise "De Ulixis erroribus" (Obsopoeus 1531, Gessner 1542) was printed under his name, but it is Manuel Gabalas' Epitomos diegesis. That work exists in Latin, French, Spanish and Portuguese, but only partly in English. Gabalas' longer prose Planai tou Odysseos (Vind. theol. gr. 174, ff. 88r–116v) is about three-quarters unedited; only the Circe and Hades parts are transcribed (Browning 1992; Vianès-Abou Samra 2003). It is listed here as context only.

Moschopoulos: only Iliad 1–2 scholia were found, nothing on the Odyssey. No edited Byzantine prose paraphrase of the Odyssey was found, apart from the Demosthenes Thrax fragments quoted by Eustathius (Nünlist, KUPS). Planudes and the Etymologica: nothing Odyssey-specific was verified (context only).

Psellos, Homeric allegories, translated by А.В. Гараджа, so drop them:
- Tantalus, Sphinx, Cave of the Nymphs, Odysseus and Circe: ΣΧΟΛΗ 19.2 (2025) 1204–1224.
- 'Assembly of the gods' (Il. 4) and 'golden chain' (Il. 8): ΣΧΟΛΗ 20.1 (2026) 447–460 (classics.nsu.ru/schole).

Malalas Book V (Troy/Odysseus): Russian by Л.А. Фрейберг, 1968, according to Кобзева 2017 (scope to verify). The Belgorod series (Болгов et al., «Мир поздней античности») covers books XIII–XVIII (2014) and others.

Lycophron's Alexandra: only excerpts in ВДИ 1947; the scholia are not translated.

Eustathius (preface, books 1–24), Tzetzes' Allegories of the Odyssey, Gabalas' Epitome and Prologue, and Eudocia's centos: no Russian translation found.

S., «Гомер как первый богослов: аллегория и символ в трактате Порфирия «О пещере нимф»», Вестник ПСТГУ III, вып. 64 (2020), 47–66, n. 31, gives a one-sentence Russian paraphrase of Eustathius' verdict that Porphyry "talked much nonsense in elegant words" about the cave (Stallbaum II p. 41.35–36). (3) «К вопросу о знаках возвращения Одиссея» (ИЯКФ, 2017) translates short Eustathius passages, but on Od. 11 (the oar), not Book 13.

(1) The Brill series page (brill.com/display/serial/ECOT, Cullhed & Olson) lists only three volumes: Vol. I, 27 Oct 2022, Rh. 1–4, ISBN 978-90-04-52735-5; Vol. II, 13 Jul 2023, Rh. 5–8, ISBN 978-90-04-54870-1; Vol. III, 18 Dec 2025 (copyright 2026), Rh. 9–12, ISBN 978-90-04-72794-6. Beatrice, "Homer's Philosophy of the Soul", in The Philosophy of the Few against the Christians (Brill 2023). It is paywalled; any translated excerpt is unverified. verification.source_text:
The best open text is Stallbaum (ed.), Eustathii archiepiscopi Thessalonicensis Commentarii ad Homeri Odysseam, vol. II, Leipzig: Weigel, 1826 (archive.org metadata gives 1825). It is public domain and online at https://archive.org/details/commentariiadhom02eust (University of Toronto copy). OCR: https://archive.org/download/commentariiadhom02eust/commentariiadhom02eust_djvu.txt.
I located Book 13 in the scan. It runs from Stallbaum II p. 35/36 (hypothesis "Κοιμώμενον Ὀδυσσέα μετὰ τῶν δώρων ἐκτιθέασιν οἱ Φαίακες…", heading ΟΔΥΣΣΕΙΑΣ Ν) to about p. 58; Book Ξ's running heads begin on p. 59. In the Rome edition this is roughly pp. 1730/31–1748. The Porphyry paraphrase (cave = cosmos, Naiads = souls going into birth, bowls and amphorae = bodies, looms = flesh, bees and honey, Cancer and Capricorn as the two gates) is at Stallbaum II pp. 40–41, Rom. c. 1734.60–1735.22. Next to it come Strabo's denial that the cave exists, the etymology of Phorkys' harbour, and Eustathius' "λήρων" verdict.
Caveats: the OCR Greek is poor, so the text must be re-keyed or corrected against the scans. Stallbaum only reprints the Rome editio princeps (1542–50). The new Cullhed–Olson critical text (Brill), based on the autograph manuscripts (Cullhed, Mnemosyne 2012), does not yet reach Book 13 and is in copyright. The TLG text (tlg4083.tlg002) is not openly licensed.
verification.recommendation: This is a strong candidate for a Russian translation: none exists, and the Book 13 cave section is a key Byzantine witness to Porphyry's De antro. The English side is valuable only for a limited time, because Brill's online edition adds about two books a year and Book 13 is next. I suggest starting with a pilot unit of Stallbaum II pp. 40–42 (Rom. 1734–1736: the Porphyry paraphrase, Strabo and Phorkys). Then complete Book 13 (Stallbaum II pp. 35–58), translating into Russian first, publishing English alongside, and checking against Brill once Book 13 appears there.

Juan Bautista Juan-López, 'Manuel Gabalas: Biography, Intellectual Network, Works and Thought', PhD dissertation, Central European University Vienna, 2024 (supervisor Baukje van den Berg; defended 3 May 2024; 262 pp.; open access, CC BY-NC-ND 4.0). Its Appendix 5, 'The Brief Narration (A9). Edition, translation', opens with the title Ἐπίτομος διήγησις εἰς τὰς καθ᾿Ὅμηρον πλάνας τοῦ Ὀδυσσέως… τῆς τῶν νέων εἵνεκεν ὠφελείας. I downloaded the PDF and checked the appendix. It edits the Greek from the autograph Vind. theol. gr. 174 (fols. 116v ff.) and Burney 114. It translates the Protheoria and all 11 chapters into English: Lotus-eaters, Polyphemus, Aeolus, Laestrygonians, Circe, Cimmerians/Hades, Sirens, Scylla and Charybdis, … and Calypso, Alcinous and return to Ithaca. That includes the ending missing from Westermann. URLs: https://biblio.ugent.be/publication/01JAJQ5CABP1FJPZA0SFGQ9NK0 (PDF: /file/01JAJQG62ZHTGSKDMG9BY716ZZ.pdf); https://www.etd.ceu.edu/2024/juan-lopez_juan.pdf. Devogge, 2020, 48–58 (https://biblio.ugent.be/publication/01JAMN8J6S2199MGH98VK6NFY6). PROLOGUE (A7): no full English translation found. Only short phrases appear in English, in B. van den Berg, 'For the love of literature: a Byzantine perspective', BMGS 49.1 (2025) 40–47 (open access, quoting Prologue 29–31 ed. BRIEF NARRATION:
- Public domain: A. Westermann, ΜΥΘΟΓΡΑΦΟΙ. Scriptores poeticae historiae Graeci (Braunschweig 1843) 329–344. Confirmed on archive.org, marked NOT_IN_COPYRIGHT: https://archive.org/details/mythographoiscri00westuoft (also mythographoi00west). This text descends from Obsopoeus/Columbus (the Burney-type version) and lacks the ending.
- Supplement, also public domain: R. Hercher, 'Zu Nicephoros Gregoras de Erroribus Ulixis', Philologus 8 (1853) 755–57, which collates the Vienna manuscript.
- Best critical text: Juan-López 2024 dissertation, Appendix 5, edited from the autograph Vind. theol. gr. 174 and Burney 114. It is CC BY-NC-ND 4.0, so it is fine for reference and collation, but the edition itself is no-derivatives.

PROLOGUE:
- Public domain: P. Matranga, Anecdota Graeca II (Rome 1850). Juan-López gives the pages as 520–24; the brief's 540–542 should be checked. Also PG 149, 664B–668A.
- Critical edition, in copyright: Silvano, JÖB 67 (2017) 217–37.
verification.recommendation: The claim that the Brief Narration is untranslated is refuted. It has a complete English translation (Juan-López, open-access 2024 dissertation), two French translations, a full Portuguese one and two Latin ones, so it should only be considered for a Russian-only edition, made from Westermann 1843 checked against Juan-López's collations. For a genuinely new Neoscholia text, the short Laudatory Prologue is better: no Russian or English translation, and Matranga/PG are public domain. Start there, then pursue Gabalas' untranslated 15-episode prose 'Wanderings of Odysseus' (A8) one episode at a time, after clearing the CC BY-NC-ND edition with Juan-López or working from the Vienna autograph.

verification.source_text:
Public domain, and the sweep's citation needs correcting: P. Matranga, Anecdota Graeca, vol. I (Rome: Bertinelli, 1850), pp. 224–~296. This is archive.org item anecdotagraecaem01matruoft (https://archive.org/details/anecdotagraecaem01matruoft), flagged NOT_IN_COPYRIGHT. I checked it in the OCR. It prints «Ἰωάννου γραμματικοῦ τοῦ Τζέτζου Ἀλληγορίαι εἰς τὴν Ὀδύσσειαν» from the proem through Book 13, which breaks off mid-book; Heraclitus' Homeric Allegories follows on pp. ~296ff. Books 9–12 run from about p. 273 (hypothesis of Book 9) to p. 293, so the whole unit is in this public-domain text. The Malalas-based Cyclops passage is there, with Polyphemus' daughter Elpe and Sicily.
The sweep's "Anecdota Graeca II, 599–618" is wrong for this purpose. Those pages, in archive item anecdotagraecaem02matruoft, carry the running heads "In prooemium allegoriarum" and "Ad allegorias Iliadis": they are scholia on the Allegories of the Iliad.
Critical edition: H. Hunger, "Johannes Tzetzes, Allegorien zur Odyssee, Buch 1–12. Kommentierte Textausgabe", BZ 49 (1956) 249–310, doi:10.1515/byzs.1956.49.2.249. Books 13–24 are in BZ 48 (1955) 4–48, doi:10.1515/byzs.1955.48.1.4. Both are published by De Gruyter, and Hunger died in 2000, so the introduction and commentary are in copyright. Whether the edited Greek text is itself protected needs legal review. Germany's special right for scholarly editions (§70 UrhG) lasts only 25 years, but this is not settled for an Austrian editor. The DOML facing Greek text is also under copyright.
Practical route: use Matranga as the base text and correct it against Hunger 1956 and the DOML readings.
verification.recommendation: The text is untranslated into Russian, which meets priority 1, but a complete English translation exists (DOML 56, 2019, all 24 books), so it fails the "ideally no English" goal. Treat it as a Russian-only, medium-priority candidate. If it goes ahead, Books 9–12 (Cyclops, Aeolus, Laestrygonians, Circe, Nekyia, Sirens, Scylla) are a good first unit: about 20 pages of political verse, fully covered by the public-domain Matranga I (1850) text, to be checked against Hunger 1956 and with the DOML translation available for verification.

verification.source_text:
Public domain: G. Stallbaum (ed.), Eustathii … Commentarii ad Homeri Odysseam, vol. II (Leipzig: Weigel, 1826), https://archive.org/details/commentariiadhom02eust (University of Toronto scan). Verified from its OCR:
- The volume covers Od. 12–24, Rom. 1705–1970.
- Od. 19 runs Rom. 1853–1880, about 23k Greek tokens.
- The dreams/gates note on 19.560ff. is at Rom. 1877–1878. It cites several interpretations (horn = eyes; heavenly vs chthonic dreams) and 'the Italian' (Ἰταλός, presumably John Italos) on dreams.
- Od. 23 runs about Rom. 1936–1950 (~12k tokens) and Od. 24 runs Rom. 1950–1970 (~15k tokens), ending at 'Τέλος'.
The Aristarchus/Aristophanes τέλος note on 23.296 falls at the bottom of Rom. 1948, just before the 1949 marker. That fits the standard citation '1948.49', but the OCR there is garbled, so check the page images. Brill's new critical text (Cullhed & Olson) is in copyright and will replace Stallbaum. Pair with Dindorf's Scholia Graeca in Homeri Odysseam (1855, PD) for these books, which Pontani's edition has not yet reached.
verification.recommendation: A good Russian candidate, but in English it is a gap only until Brill reaches Od. 19 (about 2028) and Od. 23–24 (about 2030). Start with the Od. 19.535–604 commentary (Penelope's dream and the gates of horn and ivory, Rom. ~1875–1878, ~3–4k words), then the 23.296 τέλος note plus the start of Book 24 on the second Nekyia (Rom. 1948–1952), aimed mainly at Russian readers.
