verification.ru_found:
I found no Russian translation of the commentary, whole or in part, and nothing that amounts to one. The colleague's "none" is wrong only in a technical sense: one scholarly article quotes a few sentences in Russian.
(1) Т. С. Каухчишвили, «О некоторых сведениях Ликофрона и его схолиастов» (Кавказ и Средиземноморье, Тбилиси 1980, с. 102–108), online at https://ancientrome.ru/publik/article.htm?a=1703369030 . It gives short Russian renderings of Tzetzes. One falls inside the Odysseus section: his note on moly at vv. 679–680 (moly as the plant that saved Odysseus from Circe, its etymology, physicians identifying it as wild rue, and its use against magic). The others are on vv. 174/887 (Colchians as "Indian Scythians" near the Abasgi), 1312 (Ligystic/Libystic), and mentions of 648–649. That is about 100–150 words in total, quoted for Georgian/Colchian questions.
(2) Д. О. Торшилов's commentary to Гигин, «Мифы» (СПб., 2000) cites "Цец. Комментарий к «Александре» Ликофрона" on vv. 653 (Sirens), 772 (Pan) and 45 (Scylla), as Russian Wikipedia's notes show. These are references to the myth variants, not translations.
(3) ancientrome.ru's Lycophron page (https://ancientrome.ru/antlitr/lykophron/index.htm) has only Суриков's translation of the poem (ВДИ 2011 №1–2) and articles by Мосолкин and Каухчишвили. Суриков's preface lists editions of the poem only. No scholia are translated.
(4) Латышев, «Известия древних писателей о Скифии и Кавказе» (ВДИ 1947 №3, с. 265–266) translates only lines of the poem. Russian Wikipedia's page on Tzetzes lists Russian excerpts only from «Памятники византийской литературы IX–XIV вв.» (1969, с. 252–259). I did not check which Tzetzes works that anthology contains.
verification.en_found:
There is a complete English version, but it is a machine translation with no published human translation behind it.
ToposText work 860 (https://topostext.org/work/860), checked 2026-10-05, covers the whole commentary, from Tzetzes' prolegomena to v. 1471. It has 137 entries for vv. 648–819, including 712–737 on the Sirens and Parthenope and 805 on Odysseus' grave at Perge. Its own note says it was "translated by CHATGPT 4.0 with more speed than accuracy", with prompts by Bruce Hartzler and "a few manual improvements (?)" by Brady Kiesling. The Greek source it links to is the archive.org scan of Scheer vol. II.
Human English translations of parts:
- Attalus.org (Andrew Smith) translates the Life of Lycophron from Tzetzes' prolegomena (https://www.attalus.org/poetry/lives.html). This is not the Odysseus section.
- Theoi.com's Sirens page lists "Tzetzes on Lycophron 712" under "Other references not currently quoted here", so it has no translation.
- Mair (Loeb 1921), Mooney (1921), Hornblower (OUP 2015 edition and commentary; Oxford World's Classics 2022) and McNelis & Sens (2016) translate the poem. Their notes draw on and sometimes paraphrase the scholia. I could not check how much scholia text Hornblower translates verbatim.
So EN is "full" only as an unreviewed machine translation.

I found no modern-language translation of the commentary itself. Everything listed translates the poem; some of these works use the scholia in their notes.
- German: G. Schade, Lykophrons 'Odyssee': Alexandra 648–819 übersetzt und kommentiert (De Gruyter 1999, TuK 20). F. Horn (ed.), Lykophron, Alexandra griechisch–deutsch (Tusculum, De Gruyter 2021/22, doi 10.1515/9783110754698).

- Italian: Ciaceri (1901/1983), Fusillo–Hurst–Paduano (1991), Gigante Lanzara (BUR 2000).
- Spanish: Mascialino (1956).

Canter's and Potter's Latin annotationes paraphrase Tzetzes. I checked the Potter OCR at vv. 712–719: Latin notes, not a version of Tzetzes. Müller (Leipzig 1811, 3 vols) is a Greek edition.
- Modern Greek: not verified.

Sources checked: the Hellenistic Bibliography's Lycophron page (sites.google.com/site/hellenisticbibliography/hellenistic/lycophron) and CrossRef queries in English, Italian, French and German. Neither showed any translation of the scholia.
verification.source_text:
Best source: E. Scheer, Lycophronis Alexandra, vol. II: Scholia continens (Berlin: Weidmann 1908; public domain). It is at https://archive.org/details/lycophronisalexa02lycouoft (archive.org metadata gives "volume 2 / Scholia", but the date field wrongly says 1881). This is also the source ToposText links to.
Caveat: the archive.org OCR text is unusable, because Greek OCR was run over the Latin as well. The page images would need fresh Greek OCR, or the Greek could be taken from the TLG for checking only.
Other public-domain witnesses:
- C. G. Müller, Isaakiou kai Iōannou tou Tzetzou eis Lykophrona (Leipzig 1811, 3 vols): https://archive.org/details/bub_gb_DPVDAAAAYAAJ
- Potter (Oxford 1702), with Tzetzes in Greek and Latin notes: https://archive.org/details/bub_gb_1saTNzUwiEsC
- Bachmann, Scholia vetusta (1848), on archive.org.
Leone's 2002 Congedo edition covers only the old scholia and paraphrases, and is in copyright.
verification.recommendation: A good secondary candidate. No human translation of Tzetzes on Lycophron exists in any modern language: Russian has only a few sentences in Каухчишвили 1980, and the only full English is a self-confessedly rough ChatGPT-4 version. A vetted Russian and English version with commentary, set beside ToposText's draft, would show what Neoscholia's method adds. Its link to the Odyssey is indirect: a Byzantine commentary on a Hellenistic poem that reworks the Odyssey. Start with Tzetzes on vv. 712–737 (Sirens, the Parthenope cult at Naples, the Timaeus fragment on Diotimus' torch race; about 2–3k words). Then do 648–711 (overview, Cyclops, Circe/moly, Nekyia) and 738–819 (Calypso, return, Pan son of Penelope, Telegonus and Odysseus' graves).

verification.title: Homerocentones / Ὁμηρόκεντρα (Homeric Centos), attributed to Aelia Eudocia (with Patricius and later redactors), 5th c.
verification.ru_found: The sweep's "RU none" is refuted. T. L. Aleksandrova published a complete Russian translation of the long (first) redaction, the 1НС of about 2,344 lines. She built it in cento technique from Gnedich's Iliad and Zhukovsky's Odyssey, adjusting lines to stay closer to the Greek. (1) «Гомеровский центон императрицы Евдокии», Вестник ПСТГУ. Серия III: Филология, вып. 50 (2017), pp. 63–97 (translation c. pp. 73–92). This part has an introductory article on the Christian Homeric centos and a bibliography, and runs to v. 851. Article page: http://periodical.pstgu.ru/ru/series/issue/3/50/article/3587 ; CyberLeninka: https://cyberleninka.ru/article/n/gomerovskiy-tsenton-imperatritsy-evdokii (2) «Императрица Евдокия. Гомеровский центон», Вестник ПСТГУ III: Филология, вып. 55 (2018), pp. 89–125, DOI 10.15382/sturIII201855.89-125. This part covers v. 852 to the end (v. 2344, the Ascension). No further part is announced. Pages: http://periodical.pstgu.ru/ru/series/issue/3/55/article/6579 ; https://cyberleninka.ru/article/n/imperatritsa-evdokiya-gomerovskiy-tsenton. The work is also listed in Vox medii aevi's bibliography of Russian translations for 2016–2017 (https://voxmediiaevi.com/en/bibliotheca/translates20162017/). An academia.edu/ResearchGate upload is titled "The Homeric Cento by Empress Eudocia (Russian translation, part 1)". The sweep apparently saw only Aleksandrova's authorship studies. Note: the shorter or other redactions (Patricius/Optimus/Cosmas versions, Rey's text) do not appear to have their own Russian translation; that is not verified either way.
verification.en_found: The sweep's "EN full" is not supported. M. D. Usher, Homeric Stitchings: The Homeric Centos of the Empress Eudocia (Rowman & Littlefield 1998, 192 pp.), is a monograph, "the first extended study" of the poem. The BMCR review (James Holoka, 1999.09.08, https://bmcr.brynmawr.edu/1999/1999.09.08/) never mentions a translation or an appendix and describes the book as focused on narrative technique. So Usher gives translated passages within the analysis, and I found no evidence of a complete translation. His Teubner edition (1999) is Greek only. Brian Sowers, In Her Own Words: The Life and Poetry of Aelia Eudocia (CHS/Harvard 2020), studies the centos in chapter 2. Its appended "first ever complete translation into English" is of the St Cyprian poem, not the centos; this is confirmed by the BMCR review 2024.05.36 (Lygouris) and by English Wikipedia. Anna Lefteratou, The Homeric Centos: Homer and the Bible Interwoven (OUP 2023), is a study and presumably has translated passages (not verified). I found no complete English translation online (ToposText, Canopos, theoi, attalus). Caveat: my search budget ran out before I could check the Homeric Stitchings table of contents directly, so a partial appendix translation there cannot be ruled out. A complete one seems unlikely given the reviews.
verification.other_found: French: André-Louis Rey, Patricius, Eudocie, Optimus, Côme de Jérusalem. Centons homériques (Homerocentra), Sources Chrétiennes 437 (Paris: Cerf 1998). It has a critical text and a French translation; the BMCR 1999 review calls it "ed. and trans." French Wikipedia misnumbers it as SC 427. Italian: Rocco Schembra, La prima redazione dei centoni omerici. Traduzione e commento (Alessandria: Edizioni dell'Orso 2006), and La seconda redazione dei centoni omerici. Traduzione e commento (2007). The source for these is A Hellenistic Bibliography (https://sites.google.com/site/hellenisticbibliography/empire/eudocia) and Italian Wikipedia. Schembra also edited all the redactions as Homerocentones, CCSG 62 (Brepols 2007). Aleksandrova's 2017 bibliography cites Rey, Schembra and Usher. I found no Spanish, German or modern Greek translation, but I could not search these specifically after the search budget was used up.
verification.source_text: Public domain: A. Ludwich, Eudociae Augustae, Procli Lycii, Claudiani carminum graecorum reliquiae (Leipzig: Teubner 1897), which contains the Homerocentones. It is digitized at https://archive.org/details/eudociae-augustae-homerocentones-u-procli-lycii-claudiani-carminum-graecorum-by-a.-ludwich-1897 (PDF, OCR text). Ludwich's text is older, and its redaction differs from Usher's long version of about 2,344 lines. The standard modern texts are all in copyright: Usher, Teubner 1999 (the long first redaction); Rey, SC 437 (1998); and Schembra, CCSG 62 (2007), which covers all redactions. An archive.org upload of Usher 1999 exists but is not openly licensed. I found no openly licensed critical text.
verification.recommendation: Not a good Neoscholia candidate. The main (long) redaction already has a complete Russian translation (Aleksandrova, Вестник ПСТГУ III 50 and 55, 2017–2018), plus complete French (Rey 1998) and Italian (Schembra 2006–2007) translations, so it fails priority (1). At most, Neoscholia could do an English version or an Odyssey-source commentary keyed to the Russian cento translation, which is a secondary use and not a new translation.
